name: Pinkish
lede: Pinkish is a modifier more than a color: a mid-light rose, in our library from a color survey, standing for anything that leans toward pink.

sections.title: What the suffix does
sections.body:
Pinkish is [[pink]] with the suffix -ish, which Paterson's dictionary lists as an -ish form [1]. The same dictionary defines a run of colors with the word in them: a pinkish red for a Burmese ruby, a pinkish purple for clover, and the pinkish shades of human skin [1].

So the word is a qualifier, not a name. Baty describes an eighteenth-century color nomenclature that used human skin as its animal example of flesh red, which amounts to pinkish [8]. No book in our collection fixes the word to one shade.

sections.title: Where the books use it
sections.body: Writers reach for pinkish when a color has partly gone, or when pink is hiding in something else. Brazilwood dyes ran from deep crimson and purple down to a dowdy pinkish brown as they faded [3]. In old paintings, Finlay says, pinkish flesh pigments have faded and left faces a sickly green [2]. Pastoureau counts pinkish among the many whites painters used for snow and linen [4]. Among stones, a pinkish garnet is called rhodolite and a pinkish tourmaline is rubellite [5]. See [[gem:garnet|garnet]] and [[gem:tourmaline|tourmaline]].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch here, #D46A7E, comes from the xkcd color survey, where people named colors in their own words [6]. It is a mid-light rose, closer to [[rose-pink]] and [[old-rose]] than to a pale baby pink. Our app's nearest named color is [[puce]], 8.6 units away [6]. Puce in Paterson's dictionary is a dull purple or brownish purple, so the match is arithmetic, not description [1][6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Pinkish, matched within six units of CIEDE2000 and covering at least five per cent of the canvas, appears in 1 of 23,781 paintings: Botticelli's *Baptism of Saint Zenobius*, dated about 1500, where it covers 5.6 per cent [7]. It is a highlight color there, as it is in every match [7]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [7].

Where to look: at flesh in an old painting. Finlay says Roman and Byzantine artists welcomed that cooling look: face mosaics set green stones among the pink to tone down a ruddy complexion [2].

origin.named_after: pink plus the suffix -ish; no single coiner

openers: Pinkish is a hedge word: books use it for faded dyes, snow whites and the skin tone of a Burmese ruby.
